vulnerabilities.name: Insecure Deserialization via Java ObjectInputStream / readObject
vulnerabilities.description: Untrusted bytes are passed to Java's native ObjectInputStream (or a subclass) without a class allow-list or serialization filter, so an attacker can instantiate arbitrary classes available on the classpath and trigger unintended code paths during deserialization.
vulnerabilities.notes: Not a finding if an ObjectInputFilter allow-list, a resolveClass override restricting classes, or an HMAC integrity check precedes deserialization. Prefer data-only formats (JSON without polymorphic typing).

vulnerabilities.name: Java Serialized Object Magic Bytes in Request, Cookie, or Parameter
vulnerabilities.description: A request or response carries a Java serialized stream, recognizable by the magic bytes AC ED 00 05 (hex) or rO0AB (Base64) or H4sIAAAAAAAA followed by rO0 (gzip + Base64). This shows that the application exchanges native serialized objects with the client and deserializes them server-side.

reflection_indicators.rO0AB[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{10,}: Base64-encoded Java serialized stream in a hidden field, parameter, or response body
reflection_indicators.(%AC%ED%00%05|\\\\xac\\\\xed\\\\x00\\\\x: raw or hex-encoded Java serialization header
reflection_indicators.H4sIAAAAAAAA[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{20,}: gzip-compressed Base64 blob that may wrap a serialized object (decode to check)

vulnerabilities.notes: Indicator only. Decode the value and check for the AC ED 00 05 header. A match justifies deeper testing of the consuming endpoint but is not proof of exploitability.

vulnerabilities.name: Insecure Deserialization via Python pickle/marshal/shelve/dill
vulnerabilities.description: Untrusted data is loaded with pickle, cPickle, dill, shelve, marshal, or joblib/numpy loaders that execute pickle opcodes. The pickle format can invoke arbitrary callables during load, so any attacker-controlled input yields code execution.
vulnerabilities.notes: Also flag pickle loads of data from shared caches (Redis, Memcached), message queues, and user-uploaded model files, because anyone able to write to those stores controls the payload. Use HMAC-signed payloads or a safe format such as JSON or safetensors.

vulnerabilities.name: Python Pickle Stream Indicator in Request, Cookie, or Response
vulnerabilities.description: A cookie, parameter, or body value looks like a Base64-encoded Python pickle (protocol 2 to 5 headers such as gAJ, gASV, gANj, or the ASCII protocol-0 prefix), indicating that the application round-trips pickled objects through the client.

reflection_indicators.gASV[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{12,}: Base64 of a protocol-4 pickle (starts with 0x80 0x04 0x95)
reflection_indicators.gAJ[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{12,}: Base64 of a protocol-2 pickle (starts with 0x80 0x02)
reflection_indicators.gANj[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{8,}: Base64 of a protocol-3 pickle that begins by importing a global
reflection_indicators.(\\\\x80\\\\x0[2-5]|%80%0[2-5]): raw or percent-encoded pickle protocol header

vulnerabilities.notes: Indicator only. Decode the Base64 value and inspect the first bytes. Server-side session storage with a signed ID is safe; client-side pickled sessions are not.

vulnerabilities.name: Insecure Deserialization via PHP unserialize() and phar:// Wrapper
vulnerabilities.description: User-controlled data reaches PHP unserialize(), enabling PHP object injection through magic methods (__wakeup, __destruct, __toString). File functions that accept an attacker-influenced path can also trigger deserialization of phar archive metadata through the phar:// stream wrapper.
vulnerabilities.notes: Safer: unserialize($data, ['allowed_classes' => false]) or JSON. For phar issues, validate and normalize user-supplied paths and block the phar:// scheme. Exploitability depends on available classes with dangerous magic methods (autoloaded frameworks and libraries).

vulnerabilities.name: PHP Serialized Object Indicator in Request, Cookie, or Response
vulnerabilities.description: A parameter, cookie, or response field matches PHP's serialize() format (for example O:4:"User":2:{...}, a:2:{...}) either in plain text, URL-encoded, or Base64, showing that PHP objects are exchanged with the client.

reflection_indicators.O:\\d+:\"[A-Za-z_\\\\][A-Za-z0-9_\\\\]*\: PHP serialized object in plain text
reflection_indicators.a:\\d+:\\{(i:\\d+|s:\\d+:\"[^\"]*\");: PHP serialized array in plain text
reflection_indicators.Tzo[0-9]+OiI[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{8,}: Base64 of a PHP serialized object (prefix O:)
reflection_indicators.YTo[0-9]+OnN[A-Za-z0-9+/=]{4,}|YToy[A-Za: Base64 of a PHP serialized array (prefix a:)

vulnerabilities.notes: Indicator only. Modify a harmless field (such as a string length or a boolean) and observe the application's behavior or error output to confirm that the value is deserialized.

vulnerabilities.name: Insecure Deserialization via .NET BinaryFormatter, NetDataContractSerializer, LosFormatter, SoapFormatter, ObjectStateFormatter
vulnerabilities.description: Untrusted data is deserialized by a .NET formatter that can instantiate arbitrary types. BinaryFormatter is considered dangerous and cannot be made safe; the other listed formatters carry the same class of risk.
vulnerabilities.notes: Json.NET with TypeNameHandling other than None is unsafe on untrusted input unless a restrictive SerializationBinder (allow-list) is used. Microsoft recommends removing BinaryFormatter entirely; it is disabled by default in recent .NET versions.

vulnerabilities.name: ASP.NET ViewState Without MAC Protection or With Exposed Machine Keys
vulnerabilities.description: ASP.NET __VIEWSTATE is deserialized on postback. If MAC validation is disabled, ViewState encryption is off, or the machineKey validation/decryption keys are weak, default, or leaked, an attacker can forge a malicious ViewState that is deserialized by the server.

reflection_indicators.<input[^>]+name=[\"']__VIEWSTATE[\"'][^>: unencrypted ViewState (/wEP prefix) exposed in the page, which indicates encryption is not enabled
reflection_indicators.<input[^>]+name=[\"']__VIEWSTATEGENERATO: ViewState generator field present (page uses ViewState)
reflection_indicators.<input[^>]+name=[\"']__VIEWSTATE[\"'](?!: very short ViewState value that may indicate disabled or weak protection

vulnerabilities.notes: A ViewState beginning with /wEP is not encrypted, and decoding it can disclose application data. Exploitability needs a missing MAC or access to the machine keys (for example from a leaked web.config or published sample key).

vulnerabilities.name: Unsafe Polymorphic Deserialization in Java JSON/XML Libraries (Jackson, Fastjson, XStream, SnakeYAML)
vulnerabilities.description: A Java data-binding library is configured to honor type information from the input (default typing, @class/@type fields, autoType, or unrestricted XStream/SnakeYAML constructors), so an attacker can pick which class gets instantiated and which setters or constructors run.
vulnerabilities.notes: Safe patterns: PolymorphicTypeValidator with an explicit allow-list for Jackson, SafeConstructor for SnakeYAML, XStream security framework with an allow-list, and no autoType for Fastjson (or Fastjson 2 safe mode).

vulnerabilities.name: Insecure YAML Deserialization (Python/Ruby/PHP/Node Unsafe Loaders)
vulnerabilities.description: Untrusted YAML is parsed with a loader that supports language-specific object tags (such as !!python/object or !ruby/object), letting an attacker instantiate arbitrary objects or call functions during parsing.
vulnerabilities.notes: Use yaml.safe_load in Python, YAML.safe_load with permitted_classes in Ruby (Psych 4 makes load safe by default), and js-yaml 4+ (safe by default). Flag third-party config or upload endpoints that accept YAML.

vulnerabilities.name: Insecure Deserialization via Ruby Marshal.load
vulnerabilities.description: Untrusted data is passed to Marshal.load/Marshal.restore (or a cookie store that uses Marshal), allowing attacker-chosen objects to be instantiated. Rails applications with a leaked secret_key_base and a Marshal cookie serializer are especially exposed.

reflection_indicators.BAh[A-Za-z0-9+/=%-]{8,}: Base64 of a Ruby Marshal stream (starts with 0x04 0x08)

vulnerabilities.notes: Use :json as the cookies serializer and keep secret_key_base secret and out of version control. A hard-coded secret_key_base in a repository is a finding by itself.

vulnerabilities.name: Unsafe Deserialization and Prototype Pollution in Node.js (node-serialize, serialize-to-js, Object Merging)
vulnerabilities.description: Untrusted data is passed to libraries that evaluate serialized functions (node-serialize, serialize-to-js, funcster) or is recursively merged into existing objects without blocking __proto__, constructor, and prototype keys, leading to code execution or global object tampering.

reflection_indicators._\\$\\$ND_FUNC\\$\\$_: node-serialize function marker present in a cookie or parameter

vulnerabilities.notes: For prototype pollution, flag merges where keys come from untrusted JSON without filtering __proto__, constructor, and prototype (or without using Object.create(null) or a safe merge library). Confirm behavior safely by checking whether a harmless property set through __proto__ appears on unrelated objects.

vulnerabilities.name: Insecure Deserialization via Python jsonpickle / PyYAML-like Object-Restoring JSON
vulnerabilities.description: jsonpickle.decode (and similar libraries) rebuild Python objects from JSON that includes type markers such as py/object and py/reduce. Untrusted JSON can therefore instantiate arbitrary classes and call arbitrary functions.
vulnerabilities.notes: Replace jsonpickle with plain json plus explicit schema validation (for example pydantic or marshmallow) for any data that crosses a trust boundary.

vulnerabilities.name: Deserialization Error Message Disclosure
vulnerabilities.description: Modified or malformed serialized data triggers a language-specific deserialization error in the response. This confirms that the input reaches a deserializer and often reveals the library, class names, and file paths that guide further testing.

reflection_indicators.java\\.lang\\.ClassNotFoundException|Cla: Java class resolution or cast error during deserialization
reflection_indicators.invalid stream header: [0-9A-Fa-f]{8}: Java ObjectInputStream rejected the stream header (confirms native deserialization)
reflection_indicators.__PHP_Incomplete_Class: PHP object of an unknown class was created by unserialize
reflection_indicators.Invalid length for a Base-64 char array|: ASP.NET ViewState or Base64 decoding error
reflection_indicators.SyntaxError: Unexpected token[^\\n]{0,80: Node.js JSON parse error on user-controlled data

vulnerabilities.notes: Errors help distinguish deserialization from other parsing layers. An error such as 'invalid stream header' after changing the first bytes of a Base64 value is a strong sign of native Java deserialization.

vulnerabilities.name: Serialized Session or Cookie Data Without Integrity Protection
vulnerabilities.description: Application state (user identity, roles, privileges) is stored client-side in a serialized or Base64-encoded structure with no HMAC or signature, or the signing secret is weak or default. An attacker can tamper with the serialized data to change privileges or to feed a malicious object to the deserializer.
vulnerabilities.notes: Flag cookie values that decode to an object structure and have no accompanying signature (for example a dot-separated HMAC segment or a separate signature cookie). Default or guessable secrets make signed values forgeable.

vulnerabilities.name: Deserialization Hardening Gap: No Class Allow-List, Filter, or Integrity Check Near Deserialization
vulnerabilities.description: The codebase or configuration lacks defense-in-depth for deserialization: no JEP 290 serial filter, no look-ahead ObjectInputStream, no signed payloads, no restricted loaders, and verbose errors enabled. Even if no exploitable gadget exists today, a future dependency update can introduce one.
vulnerabilities.notes: Mitigation-gap finding, not a direct vulnerability. Combine with a confirmed deserialization sink and source. Wildcard trusted packages in messaging libraries (JMS, Kafka, ActiveMQ) are a common real-world cause of deserialization exposure.
